title: UIKit Essentials & SwiftUI Interop
scopeHtml: Scope: UIViewController lifecycle, UIView, Auto Layout, UITableView/UICollectionView, delegates, UIHostingController, UIViewRepresentable.

notes.title: Baseline and why UIKit still matters
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Android you moved from Views/XML to Compose but still ship Activity, Fragment, RecyclerView and View code in old modules. iOS is the same story: SwiftUI is the future, UIKit is the foundation it is built on and still runs most big apps.

This track assumes Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials. Modern code uses @Observable, NavigationStack, async/await, actors, and Swift Testing. Where you see ObservableObject, NavigationView, completion handlers or XCTest, it is labelled "you will meet this in old codebases".

Why you still need UIKit as an Android developer joining an iOS team:

  • Instagram, Uber, Airbnb, Spotify, LinkedIn and most apps older than 2020 are largely UIKit. You will read it daily.
  • Many SwiftUI features are thin wrappers over UIKit (List on iOS 16+ is backed by UICollectionView; TextEditor, TabView and NavigationStack use UIKit controllers underneath). Debugging them means knowing UIKit.
  • Some capabilities have no SwiftUI equivalent yet: camera preview layers, WKWebView, MKMapView advanced features, PHPicker customisation, complex text editing (UITextView with TextKit), custom collection layouts. You bridge to UIKit.

Mapping the big concepts:

Android iOS (UIKit)
Activity / Fragment UIViewController
View UIView
ViewGroup UIView with subviews (any view can have children)
ConstraintLayout Auto Layout (NSLayoutConstraint)
LinearLayout UIStackView
RecyclerView + ListAdapter UICollectionView + diffable data source
ListView (old) UITableView
Application class UIApplicationDelegate / @main App
AndroidView { } in Compose UIViewRepresentable
ComposeView in a Fragment UIHostingController

Real industry examples. Airbnb open-sourced Epoxy (UIKit/Android) and later ViewEnvironment; Uber's RIBs architecture is UIKit-era; Spotify and Instagram migrate screen by screen using hosting controllers. Nobody rewrites a 10-year-old app in one go.

Analogy. UIKit is the old stone foundation of a house; SwiftUI is the new extension. You can build new rooms in the extension, but when the plumbing leaks you go to the basement.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "UIKit is deprecated". It is not; Apple still ships new UIKit APIs every year.
  • Treating UIViewController as only a "screen". It is also a lifecycle owner, a container, and a coordinator of transitions.
  • Android vs iOS: assuming there is a Manifest declaring screens. iOS has no such registry; view controllers are just objects you create and present.

notes.title: UIViewController lifecycle vs Activity and Fragment
notes.html:
Android equivalent. An Activity has onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onDestroy, and a Fragment adds onCreateView/onDestroyView. In iOS a UIViewController has a much smaller set, and the system does not kill and recreate it on configuration change.

The main callbacks, in order:

init (you create it)
  |
loadView()            <- creates self.view (rarely overridden)
viewDidLoad()         <- view exists, ONCE per lifetime: set up subviews, bind
viewIsAppearing(_:)   <- iOS 17+: view is in hierarchy with correct size/traits
viewWillAppear(_:)    <- about to be shown, every time
viewDidAppear(_:)     <- fully visible: start animations, analytics, timers
viewWillLayoutSubviews()
viewDidLayoutSubviews()  <- frame sizes final, can be called many times
viewWillDisappear(_:)
viewDidDisappear(_:)  <- stop work here
deinit                <- object freed (ARC reached zero)

viewIsAppearing(_:) is new in iOS 17 (back-deployed to iOS 13 by UIKit per Apple's WWDC23 notes; verify the exact back-deployment claim). It fixes a long-standing pain: in viewWillAppear the view's geometry and trait collection may not be final, so people put layout-dependent code in the wrong place.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
final class ProfileViewController: UIViewController {
    private let viewModel: ProfileViewModel
    private var task: Task<Void, Never>?

    init(viewModel: ProfileViewModel) {
        self.viewModel = viewModel
        super.init(nibName: nil, bundle: nil)
    }
    required init?(coder: NSCoder) { fatalError("init(coder:) not used") }

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()
        view.backgroundColor = .systemBackground
        // build UI once
    }

    override func viewDidAppear(_ animated: Bool) {
        super.viewDidAppear(animated)
        task = Task { [weak self] in
            guard let self else { return }
            for await state in viewModel.states { render(state) }
        }
    }

    override func viewDidDisappear(_ animated: Bool) {
        super.viewDidDisappear(animated)
        task?.cancel()
    }
}
class ProfileFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_profile) {
    private val viewModel: ProfileViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onViewCreated(view, savedInstanceState)
        // build UI once per view creation
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                viewModel.state.collect { render(it) }
            }
        }
    }
}

Key differences from Android:

  • No process-death or rotation recreation. Rotation resizes the same controller; viewDidLoad is not called again. No onSaveInstanceState dance for rotation. State restoration across app kill is a separate opt-in mechanism.
  • viewDidLoad is once; viewWillAppear is each time. A common bug is subscribing to a stream in viewWillAppear and never unsubscribing, leading to duplicate updates.
  • Memory warnings. didReceiveMemoryWarning() is called under pressure; the system may purge view only in very old iOS (pre-6). Today you drop caches yourself.
  • Container controllers. UINavigationController, UITabBarController and UISplitViewController own child controllers. Custom containers must call addChild, didMove(toParent:), willMove(toParent:) and removeFromParent correctly or lifecycle callbacks stop arriving.
  • Parent/child forwarding. Appearance callbacks propagate to children automatically when you use the child-controller API; adding a child's view as a subview without addChild breaks that.

Production incident pattern. super omission: forgetting super.viewWillAppear(animated) in a navigation-embedded controller produces subtle glitches (nav bar not updating, child controllers silent). Another: heavy work in viewDidLoad blocks the push animation, which shows as a hang in Instruments.

Analogy. A hotel room: viewDidLoad is furnishing the room once; viewWillAppear is the guest walking in each time; deinit is the hotel demolishing the room.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting layout-dependent code (using view.bounds) in viewDidLoad, where bounds are not final.
  • Saying deinit is called when the screen disappears. It is called only when no strong references remain; a retain cycle means it never fires.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting onSaveInstanceState. iOS controllers survive rotation, so state lives in memory unless you opt into restoration.
  • Forgetting super in lifecycle overrides.

notes.title: UIView, frames, bounds and the render pipeline
notes.html:
Android equivalent. An Android View has left/top/right/bottom relative to its parent and a Canvas to draw on. A UIView has a frame (in parent coordinates), bounds (own coordinates), center, and is backed by a CALayer that is what the GPU actually composites.

Core facts:

  • frame = position and size in the superview's coordinate space. bounds = the view's own coordinate space (origin normally (0,0); changing bounds.origin is how UIScrollView scrolls).
  • Units are points, not pixels. A 3x device (iPhone Pro) renders 3 pixels per point. This is similar to dp but fixed per device class rather than a continuous density bucket.
  • Every UIView owns a CALayer (Core Animation). Properties such as cornerRadius, shadow, borderWidth live on the layer. Animations (UIView.animate) change layer properties and the render server composites them off the main thread, which is why animations stay smooth when the main thread is busy.
  • Views are reference types (classes) and are expensive relative to SwiftUI views (structs). Roughly, thousands of UIViews in a hierarchy cost real memory.
  • Drawing: override draw(_ rect:) for Core Graphics custom drawing; call setNeedsDisplay() to request a redraw. Do not call draw yourself.
  • Layout invalidation: setNeedsLayout() schedules a layout pass for the next run loop; layoutIfNeeded() forces it now. This is analogous to requestLayout() and measure/layout.
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
final class BadgeView: UIView {
    private let label = UILabel()

    override init(frame: CGRect) {
        super.init(frame: frame)
        layer.cornerRadius = 8
        layer.masksToBounds = true   // clips; triggers offscreen pass if combined with shadow
        backgroundColor = .systemRed
        label.textColor = .white
        label.font = .preferredFont(forTextStyle: .caption1)
        addSubview(label)
    }
    required init?(coder: NSCoder) { fatalError() }

    override func layoutSubviews() {
        super.layoutSubviews()
        label.frame = bounds.insetBy(dx: 6, dy: 2)
    }
}
class BadgeView(context: Context) : FrameLayout(context) {
    private val label = TextView(context)

    init {
        background = GradientDrawable().apply {
            cornerRadius = 8.dp
            setColor(Color.RED)
        }
        label.setTextColor(Color.WHITE)
        addView(label)
    }

    override fun onLayout(changed: Boolean, l: Int, t: Int, r: Int, b: Int) {
        label.layout(6.dp, 2.dp, width - 6.dp, height - 2.dp)
    }
}

Off-screen rendering. Setting cornerRadius plus masksToBounds plus a shadow forces the GPU to render the layer into a separate buffer, which is a classic scrolling-jank cause. Fixes: set shadowPath, use CAShapeLayer masks, or pre-render. Xcode's "Color Off-screen Rendered" debug option highlights these in yellow.

Main thread rule. All UIKit access must occur on the main thread. In Swift 6, UIView and UIViewController are @MainActor, so the compiler errors when you touch them from background code, a better story than Android's runtime CalledFromWrongThreadException.

Analogy. A UIView is a transparent sticker, its layer is the physical sticker sheet the print shop (GPU) handles; you rearrange stickers cheaply without reprinting.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing frame and bounds; a rotated view has a meaningless frame (it becomes the bounding box).
  • Saying points equal pixels.
  • Updating UI from URLSession completion handlers on a background queue (pre-async code) and getting random crashes or purple runtime warnings.
  • Android vs iOS: assuming a view must be removed to be hidden; isHidden = true keeps it in the hierarchy, and inside a UIStackView hiding collapses its space.

notes.title: Auto Layout, stack views and safe area
notes.html:
Android equivalent. ConstraintLayout with constraints between siblings and parent, plus LinearLayout weights. Auto Layout is the same idea: a system of linear equations solved by the Cassowary algorithm.

Constraints are view1.attribute = multiplier * view2.attribute + constant with a priority (0 to 1000; 1000 is required). A layout is valid when every view has an unambiguous position and size.

Modern syntax uses layout anchors:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
let title = UILabel()
title.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false   // mandatory in code
view.addSubview(title)

NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
    title.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.topAnchor, constant: 16),
    title.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.leadingAnchor, constant: 16),
    title.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.trailingAnchor, constant: -16)
])
val title = TextView(context).apply { id = View.generateViewId() }
root.addView(title)

ConstraintSet().apply {
    clone(root)
    connect(title.id, ConstraintSet.TOP, ConstraintSet.PARENT_ID, ConstraintSet.TOP, 16.dp)
    connect(title.id, ConstraintSet.START, ConstraintSet.PARENT_ID, ConstraintSet.START, 16.dp)
    connect(title.id, ConstraintSet.END, ConstraintSet.PARENT_ID, ConstraintSet.END, 16.dp)
    applyTo(root)
}

Things that surprise Android developers:

  • translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false must be set for code-created views; otherwise the legacy autoresizing mask generates conflicting constraints. Forgetting it is the number one beginner bug.
  • Trailing constants are negative (-16) when pinning to the superview's trailing edge.
  • Intrinsic content size and hugging/compression priorities. A UILabel knows its own size. Content hugging resists growing; compression resistance resists shrinking. Two labels side by side with equal priorities are ambiguous; you set one's hugging priority higher to say "this one stays tight". This replaces layout_weight and wrap_content negotiations.
  • Safe area. safeAreaLayoutGuide excludes the notch, Dynamic Island, home indicator, status bar and nav bar areas. Pin content to it; pin backgrounds to the full view to draw edge to edge. This is the analogue of WindowInsets.
  • UIStackView is your LinearLayout: axis, spacing, alignment, distribution. It manages constraints for you. Hidden arranged subviews collapse automatically, a feature Android needs Group or GONE for.
  • Layout guides (UILayoutGuide) are invisible spacers, cheaper than dummy views.
  • Storyboards, XIBs are the XML analogue: visual layout files. Many legacy projects use Interface Builder with @IBOutlet and @IBAction connections; modern teams often prefer code layout because storyboards cause merge conflicts.

Debugging: a log line "Unable to simultaneously satisfy constraints" lists the conflicting constraints and which one the runtime broke. Set a symbolic breakpoint on UIViewAlertForUnsatisfiableConstraints, and give constraints identifier strings. Xcode's View Debugger (Debug > View Debugging) shows a 3D exploded hierarchy.

Performance: Auto Layout cost grows with constraint count and is roughly linear for well-formed layouts, but deeply nested self-sizing cells can be slow; Apple documents improvements since iOS 12. Avoid ambiguity and redundant constraints.

Real examples. Teams at Airbnb and Lyft used code-based layout DSLs (SnapKit, PinLayout, Lyft's layout helpers) to cut verbosity; SnapKit is a widely used library for this.

Analogy. Auto Layout is a set of springs and rulers between objects on a table: you describe relationships, not coordinates, and the table rearranges as it changes size.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false and blaming Auto Layout.
  • Pinning to the superview rather than safeAreaLayoutGuide, causing content under the Dynamic Island.
  • Saying UIStackView draws anything; it is a non-rendering layout helper.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting match_parent/wrap_content; iOS has intrinsic size plus priorities instead.

notes.title: UITableView and UICollectionView versus RecyclerView
notes.html:
Android equivalent. RecyclerView with ViewHolder, Adapter/ListAdapter and DiffUtil. In UIKit, UITableView (single column, vertical) and UICollectionView (any layout) both reuse cells.

Reuse model: you register a cell class, then ask the view to dequeue a cell for an index path. The framework hands you an old offscreen cell to reconfigure, exactly like onBindViewHolder.

Legacy way (you will meet this everywhere):

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
final class FeedViewController: UIViewController, UITableViewDataSource, UITableViewDelegate {
    private let tableView = UITableView()
    private var items: [FeedItem] = []

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()
        tableView.register(FeedCell.self, forCellReuseIdentifier: "FeedCell")
        tableView.dataSource = self
        tableView.delegate = self
        view.addSubview(tableView)
    }

    func tableView(_ tv: UITableView, numberOfRowsInSection section: Int) -> Int { items.count }

    func tableView(_ tv: UITableView, cellForRowAt indexPath: IndexPath) -> UITableViewCell {
        let cell = tv.dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier: "FeedCell", for: indexPath) as! FeedCell
        cell.configure(with: items[indexPath.row])
        return cell
    }
}
class FeedAdapter : RecyclerView.Adapter<FeedViewHolder>() {
    var items: List<FeedItem> = emptyList()

    override fun getItemCount() = items.size

    override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int) =
        FeedViewHolder(LayoutInflater.from(parent.context)
            .inflate(R.layout.item_feed, parent, false))

    override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: FeedViewHolder, position: Int) =
        holder.bind(items[position])
}

The big legacy danger: reloadData() replaces everything, and manual insertRows/deleteRows with performBatchUpdates crashes with "Invalid update: invalid number of rows in section" if your data count and your update calls disagree. That crash signature is an iOS rite of passage.

Modern replacement: diffable data source (iOS 13+). It stores identifiers, you give it snapshots, it computes the diff, like ListAdapter + DiffUtil but without you maintaining the count.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
enum Section { case main }

final class FeedViewController: UIViewController {
    private var collectionView: UICollectionView!
    private var dataSource: UICollectionViewDiffableDataSource<Section, FeedItem.ID>!

    private func configureDataSource() {
        let registration = UICollectionView.CellRegistration<FeedCell, FeedItem.ID> { cell, _, id in
            cell.configure(with: self.store[id])    // look up latest model
        }
        dataSource = .init(collectionView: collectionView) { cv, indexPath, id in
            cv.dequeueConfiguredReusableCell(using: registration, for: indexPath, item: id)
        }
    }

    func apply(_ items: [FeedItem]) {
        var snapshot = NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot<Section, FeedItem.ID>()
        snapshot.appendSections([.main])
        snapshot.appendItems(items.map(\.id))
        dataSource.apply(snapshot, animatingDifferences: true)
    }
}
class FeedAdapter : ListAdapter<FeedItem, FeedViewHolder>(Diff) {
    object Diff : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<FeedItem>() {
        override fun areItemsTheSame(a: FeedItem, b: FeedItem) = a.id == b.id
        override fun areContentsTheSame(a: FeedItem, b: FeedItem) = a == b
    }
}

adapter.submitList(items)

Notes on the diffable approach:

  • Items must be Hashable. Using whole models as items means any field change looks like delete plus insert (no row reload). Prefer identifiers as items and call snapshot.reconfigureItems([id]) (iOS 15+) or reloadItems for content changes. This mirrors areItemsTheSame vs areContentsTheSame.
  • apply is safe from background threads for the data source itself in iOS 15+ (it is documented as thread-safe if you consistently use one queue; verify for your target), but UI-touching cell code runs on main.
  • Cell registration (iOS 14+) replaces string reuse identifiers; it is type-safe.
  • Modern cell content: UIListContentConfiguration and UIContentConfiguration let a cell be configured with a value, much like Compose state-in-UI-out, and UIHostingConfiguration (iOS 16+) puts a SwiftUI view inside a cell.

Compositional layout (iOS 13+) replaces UICollectionViewFlowLayout for anything complex: you build NSCollectionLayoutItem > Group > Section with sizes .fractionalWidth, .estimated, .absolute. It supports nested horizontal carousels inside vertical lists, the App Store and Apple Music look. In Android that is ConcatAdapter plus nested RecyclerViews with GridLayoutManager.SpanSizeLookup.

let item = NSCollectionLayoutItem(layoutSize: .init(widthDimension: .fractionalWidth(1), heightDimension: .estimated(80)))
let group = NSCollectionLayoutGroup.vertical(layoutSize: .init(widthDimension: .fractionalWidth(1), heightDimension: .estimated(80)), subitems: [item])
let section = NSCollectionLayoutSection(group: group)
let layout = UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout(section: section)

Performance and prefetching: UITableViewDataSourcePrefetching and UICollectionViewDataSourcePrefetching give prefetchItemsAt and cancelPrefetchingForItemsAt so you can start image loads early. Cells must cancel their image task in prepareForReuse() or you get the classic "wrong image in reused cell" bug (same as an Android ViewHolder showing a stale image).

Real examples. Instagram's feed historically used IGListKit (diffing for UICollectionView), now less needed since diffable arrived. Kingfisher and Nuke provide cell-safe image loading.

Analogy. A sushi conveyor belt with a fixed number of plates: dishes (cells) are recycled and refilled with new food as the belt moves.

Common interview traps.

  • Dequeuing with the wrong identifier or forgetting to register, which crashes with "unable to dequeue a cell".
  • Putting mutable model structs directly in the snapshot and wondering why updates animate as remove/insert.
  • Not resetting content in prepareForReuse, showing stale images.
  • Android vs iOS: expecting ViewHolder; UIKit cells are the views themselves (subclass of UIView).

notes.title: Delegates, data sources and target-action
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Listener interfaces (OnClickListener, TextWatcher) and callbacks (Adapter interface). In iOS the dominant pattern is delegation: an object holds a reference to a helper that conforms to a protocol and calls it for events and decisions.

Two flavors:

  • Delegate answers "what happened" and "should I?" (UITextFieldDelegate.textFieldShouldReturn).
  • Data source answers "what data do you want?" (UITableViewDataSource). Splitting them keeps a clean contract.

Why delegates instead of closures? Historically Objective-C had blocks but delegates give multiple related methods, optional methods, and return values with clear names. In Swift, many modern APIs use closures or async instead, but UIKit's core remains delegate-heavy.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
protocol PaymentFormDelegate: AnyObject {
    func paymentFormDidSubmit(_ form: PaymentFormView, token: String)
}

final class PaymentFormView: UIView {
    weak var delegate: PaymentFormDelegate?   // weak to avoid a retain cycle

    @objc private func payTapped() {
        delegate?.paymentFormDidSubmit(self, token: "tok_123")
    }
}
interface PaymentFormListener {
    fun onSubmit(form: PaymentFormView, token: String)
}

class PaymentFormView(context: Context) : FrameLayout(context) {
    var listener: PaymentFormListener? = null   // weak not needed for GC, but leaks happen

    private fun payTapped() {
        listener?.onSubmit(this, "tok_123")
    }
}

The crucial rule: delegates are weak. The parent owns the child strongly (a view controller holds its table view), so the child must not own the parent back or ARC reference counts never reach zero and deinit never runs. Protocols for weak delegates are constrained with AnyObject (class-only). On Android the garbage collector copes with cycles; on iOS ARC does not collect cycles.

Other communication patterns:

  • Target-action: button.addTarget(self, action: #selector(tapped), for: .touchUpInside); the @objc selector is resolved at runtime via the Objective-C runtime. From iOS 14 you can pass a UIAction closure: UIAction { [weak self] _ in self?.tapped() }.
  • NotificationCenter: publish/subscribe broadcast, like LocalBroadcastManager (deprecated) or an event bus. Use for system events such as keyboard show/hide, UIApplication.didEnterBackgroundNotification.
  • KVO (Key-Value Observing): observes @objc dynamic properties. Swift's observe(\.keyPath) returns an NSKeyValueObservation token you must keep alive.
  • Closures capturing [weak self] for one-shot callbacks.
  • Async/await for new code: replace completion: (Result<T, Error>) -> Void with async throws -> T, bridging legacy ones with withCheckedThrowingContinuation.
func loadUser() async throws -> User {
    try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
        legacyClient.fetchUser { result in   // completion handler API
            continuation.resume(with: result)   // must resume exactly once
        }
    }
}

Resuming a continuation twice or never are both bugs: twice crashes, never leaks the awaiting task forever.

Real examples. Alamofire and older SDKs (Firebase, Stripe, Facebook SDK) expose delegates alongside closures. Apple's CLLocationManagerDelegate remains the standard way to receive location updates.

Analogy. A delegate is like handing a manager your phone number: "call me when the delivery arrives". The manager keeps the number, but must not own you, or neither of you can leave.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring var delegate: SomeDelegate? without weak, causing a retain cycle and leaked controllers.
  • Forgetting AnyObject on the protocol, so weak fails to compile.
  • Using [unowned self] and crashing when the closure outlives the object.
  • Android vs iOS: believing GC will clean cycles; ARC cannot.

notes.title: UIViewRepresentable and UIViewControllerRepresentable
notes.html:
Android equivalent. AndroidView(factory = { ... }, update = { ... }) in Compose embeds a classic View. SwiftUI's version is a protocol you conform to with makeUIView and updateUIView.

Use it when SwiftUI has no native equivalent: WKWebView, MKMapView with custom annotations, UITextView with attributed text, AVPlayerLayer, PHPickerViewController, MFMailComposeViewController, barcode scanners with AVCaptureVideoPreviewLayer.

Lifecycle of the representable:

  1. makeUIView(context:) runs once to create the UIKit view.
  2. updateUIView(_:context:) runs every time SwiftUI state used by the wrapper changes (and on first appearance). It must be idempotent and cheap.
  3. makeCoordinator() creates an object to receive delegate callbacks.
  4. dismantleUIView(_:coordinator:) is called when the view leaves the hierarchy (static, for cleanup).
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import SwiftUI
import WebKit

struct WebView: UIViewRepresentable {
    let url: URL
    @Binding var isLoading: Bool

    func makeCoordinator() -> Coordinator { Coordinator(self) }

    func makeUIView(context: Context) -> WKWebView {
        let web = WKWebView()
        web.navigationDelegate = context.coordinator
        return web
    }

    func updateUIView(_ web: WKWebView, context: Context) {
        if web.url != url { web.load(URLRequest(url: url)) }
    }

    final class Coordinator: NSObject, WKNavigationDelegate {
        var parent: WebView
        init(_ parent: WebView) { self.parent = parent }

        func webView(_ webView: WKWebView, didStartProvisionalNavigation navigation: WKNavigation!) {
            parent.isLoading = true
        }
        func webView(_ webView: WKWebView, didFinish navigation: WKNavigation!) {
            parent.isLoading = false
        }
    }
}
@Composable
fun WebViewScreen(url: String, onLoading: (Boolean) -> Unit) {
    AndroidView(
        factory = { ctx ->
            WebView(ctx).apply {
                webViewClient = object : WebViewClient() {
                    override fun onPageStarted(v: WebView, u: String, f: Bitmap?) = onLoading(true)
                    override fun onPageFinished(v: WebView, u: String) = onLoading(false)
                }
            }
        },
        update = { if (it.url != url) it.loadUrl(url) }
    )
}

Why a Coordinator? A SwiftUI struct is a value that is recreated constantly, so it cannot be a delegate (delegates need a stable reference-type object conforming to Objective-C protocols, usually NSObject). The coordinator is the stable class that survives struct re-creation and is where delegate methods live. Its parent copy is refreshed via updateUIView (set context.coordinator.parent = self there if you rely on new bindings).

Data flow rules:

  • SwiftUI to UIKit: push new values in updateUIView.
  • UIKit to SwiftUI: write to @Binding from the coordinator.
  • Writing to @Binding inside updateUIView causes "Modifying state during view update" warnings and loops; defer with Task { @MainActor in } only when truly needed.

UIViewControllerRepresentable is identical for full controllers, e.g. wrapping PHPickerViewController:

struct PhotoPicker: UIViewControllerRepresentable {
    @Binding var image: UIImage?

    func makeUIViewController(context: Context) -> PHPickerViewController {
        var config = PHPickerConfiguration()
        config.filter = .images
        let picker = PHPickerViewController(configuration: config)
        picker.delegate = context.coordinator
        return picker
    }
    func updateUIViewController(_ vc: PHPickerViewController, context: Context) {}
    func makeCoordinator() -> Coordinator { Coordinator(self) }

    final class Coordinator: NSObject, PHPickerViewControllerDelegate {
        let parent: PhotoPicker
        init(_ parent: PhotoPicker) { self.parent = parent }
        func picker(_ picker: PHPickerViewController, didFinishPicking results: [PHPickerResult]) {
            picker.dismiss(animated: true)
            // load results.first?.itemProvider ... then set parent.image on the main actor
        }
    }
}

SwiftUI sizing: representables take the size SwiftUI proposes; implement sizeThatFits(_:uiView:context:) (iOS 16+) when the UIKit view has intrinsic size needs. Verify the exact signature in current docs.

Note: SwiftUI has a native PhotosPicker (iOS 16+); prefer it for new code, and use the wrapper for features it lacks.

Analogy. A representable is a power adapter between two countries' sockets: the Coordinator is the little converter circuit that translates the signals.

Common interview traps.

  • Creating the UIKit view in updateUIView instead of makeUIView, recreating a web view on every state change.
  • Mutating UIKit state unconditionally in updateUIView, causing flicker or infinite update loops.
  • Retain cycles between coordinator and delegate-holding view; keep parent as a struct copy and the delegate weak.
  • Android vs iOS: AndroidView update lambda runs on recomposition; updateUIView likewise but with value-copy self.

notes.title: UIHostingController and embedding SwiftUI in UIKit
notes.html:
Android equivalent. ComposeView inside a Fragment or setContent { } in an Activity hosting Compose inside an existing View app. iOS equivalent: UIHostingController<Content>, a UIViewController whose view renders a SwiftUI hierarchy.

Three ways to embed:

  1. Push or present it as a controller:
let host = UIHostingController(rootView: SettingsView(viewModel: vm))
navigationController?.pushViewController(host, animated: true)
  1. As a child view controller (to place SwiftUI in a part of a screen):
let host = UIHostingController(rootView: HeaderView())
addChild(host)
host.view.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false
view.addSubview(host.view)
NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
    host.view.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.topAnchor),
    host.view.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.leadingAnchor),
    host.view.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.trailingAnchor)
])
host.didMove(toParent: self)

Skipping addChild / didMove(toParent:) breaks lifecycle, safe area and trait propagation, and causes SwiftUI onAppear oddities. This is the most common mistake.

  1. Inside a cell with UIHostingConfiguration (iOS 16+):
cell.contentConfiguration = UIHostingConfiguration {
    FeedRow(item: item)
}

This avoids a controller per cell and supports self-sizing. Apple documented it for both table and collection cells.

Self-sizing: hosting controllers report sizeThatFits. In iOS 16+, sizingOptions (e.g. .intrinsicContentSize, .preferredContentSize) controls whether the host communicates its size to Auto Layout; before iOS 16 devs used hacks calling view.invalidateIntrinsicContentSize(). Verify the available options for your SDK.

Passing data both ways: give the SwiftUI root an @Observable view model or closures (onDone: () -> Void). UIKit-to-SwiftUI changes flow through the observable object; SwiftUI-to-UIKit flows through closures or delegate-like callbacks.

Navigation interop: avoid nesting SwiftUI NavigationStack inside a UIKit UINavigationController unless you intend two nav bars to be reconciled; common strategy is to hide the SwiftUI bar or use the UIKit bar only, or have a hosting controller per screen and navigate in UIKit via a coordinator.

Migration strategy used by large teams:

  • New leaf screens in SwiftUI, hosted via UIHostingController, pushed by existing UIKit coordinators.
  • Shared design tokens (colors, fonts) exposed to both worlds.
  • Old UIKit pieces wrapped with representables when new SwiftUI parents need them.
  • Avoid wrapping a whole UIKit navigation stack in SwiftUI or vice versa halfway; pick screen-level seams.

Real examples. Airbnb, Lyft and Dropbox have written about hybrid UIKit/SwiftUI migration; Apple's own apps (Settings, Maps parts) mix both. Many teams report build-time cost when mixing, so modularise.

Analogy. A hosting controller is a picture frame screwed to a UIKit wall: the picture (SwiftUI) can change freely, but the frame must be properly fixed to the wall or the picture slides.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding host.view without addChild/didMove(toParent:).
  • Expecting UIHostingController to size itself in a stack with no constraints or sizing options.
  • Capturing a UIKit controller strongly in a SwiftUI closure, leaking both.
  • Android vs iOS: ComposeView needs a ViewCompositionStrategy; the hosting controller ties to the controller lifecycle, with no equivalent setting.

notes.title: Reading and migrating a legacy UIKit codebase
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Joining a company with a 7-year-old Java and XML app and asked to introduce Kotlin and Compose without a rewrite. The same incremental discipline applies.

First reconnaissance: what you will see in the project navigator and how to read it.

Thing in repo Meaning
AppDelegate.swift / SceneDelegate.swift App and scene lifecycle entry points (pre-SwiftUI @main App)
Main.storyboard, *.xib Interface Builder layouts (XML)
Podfile, Pods/ CocoaPods dependency manager (legacy; SPM now preferred)
Cartfile Carthage (rare)
*.xcodeproj, *.xcworkspace Project and workspace (open the workspace if Pods exist)
.m / .h files, bridging header Objective-C code interoperating with Swift
Info.plist Manifest equivalent: permissions strings, URL schemes, launch config
Assets.xcassets Drawable resources: images, colors, app icon
*.strings, .xcstrings Localization (old vs string catalog)

Common legacy patterns and what to do:

  • Massive View Controller. Thousand-line controllers doing networking, formatting and layout. Extract a view model, move formatting to pure functions, and move network calls behind a protocol. Add tests before refactoring.
  • MVC with a twist. Apple-style MVC lets controllers own models and views; the tight coupling is the reason people adopt MVVM, VIPER or Clean (see also: Architecture topic in this track).
  • Singletons everywhere (NetworkManager.shared). Introduce protocol seams and inject through initialisers.
  • Completion handler pyramids. Wrap in async using continuations; then replace call sites progressively. Remember the thread: completion handlers may not return on the main thread.
  • Combine pipelines. AnyCancellable sets, sink, assign(to:on:) (retain-cycle trap with self). Combine is not deprecated but Apple's new work targets Observation and async sequences; leave stable pipelines, write new code with async/await.
  • Objective-C interop. Swift sees Obj-C via a bridging header; Obj-C sees Swift via the generated -Swift.h header and @objc annotations. Nullability annotations (nullable/nonnull) in Obj-C headers determine whether Swift sees T? or T!.
  • Core Data. Often present; SwiftData is the modern replacement for new features but is not a drop-in migration. Leave Core Data alone unless there is a reason.
  • Swift 6 migration. Turn on strict concurrency checking incrementally (Complete checking per target) and fix warnings gradually. Mark UI types @MainActor, models Sendable. Compiler warnings under Swift 5 mode can become errors in Swift 6 mode, so migrate module by module.

Migration playbook that works in practice:

  1. Stabilise: CI builds, unit tests for critical flows, crash reporting (Crashlytics or Sentry) with dSYM upload.
  2. Add SPM modules for new code; keep legacy in the app target.
  3. Introduce view models and protocols where you change code (boy-scout rule).
  4. Build new screens in SwiftUI and host them; wrap shared legacy views as representables.
  5. Delete storyboards screen by screen once replaced; storyboards cannot be easily diffed and cause merge conflicts.
  6. Track hot paths with Instruments before optimising.

Production incident patterns in legacy UIKit:

  • Crash: NSInternalInconsistencyException in performBatchUpdates from mismatched counts; fix with diffable data source.
  • Crash: "unrecognized selector sent to instance" after renaming an @IBAction while the storyboard still references it.
  • Leak: closures or delegates retaining controllers; view memory graph debugger and Instruments Leaks show ProfileViewController instances multiplying after each navigation.
  • Hang: synchronous image decoding or JSON parse in cellForRowAt shows as a main-thread block in Instruments Time Profiler and as hangs in Xcode Organizer.
  • Layout break after OS update: dependence on private view hierarchies (e.g. fiddling with UITabBar subviews). Apple can change these between releases; avoid.

Analogy. Renovating an occupied building: you cannot demolish it; you reinforce walls room by room while tenants keep living there.

Common interview traps.

  • Suggesting a full rewrite as the first answer. Seniors propose incremental seams and measurable steps.
  • Opening the .xcodeproj when the project uses CocoaPods (must open .xcworkspace).
  • Converting every completion handler to async without handling cancellation and thread hops.
  • Android vs iOS: assuming Gradle-like transparency; Xcode project files are opaque XML and merge conflicts on project.pbxproj are common (XcodeGen or Tuist generate them).

notes.title: Interview scenarios and quick answers
notes.html:
Android equivalent. "Explain Fragment lifecycle vs Activity lifecycle" style questions; here you answer with the iOS mapping and caveats.

Typical senior questions and tight answers:

  1. "Explain the UIViewController lifecycle and where you put things." Build views in viewDidLoad; layout-sensitive work in viewIsAppearing or viewDidLayoutSubviews; start subscriptions in viewWillAppear/viewDidAppear; cancel in viewDidDisappear; cleanup relies on deinit plus no retain cycles.
  2. "How does cell reuse work and what goes wrong?" Dequeue, reconfigure, prepareForReuse cancels async work; wrong-image bug when async completion writes into a reused cell; use identifiers/tokens to verify.
  3. "Diffable data source vs reloadData?" Snapshot of identifiers, automatic diff and animation, avoids index-path crashes, reconfigureItems for content updates.
  4. "How do you add a SwiftUI screen to a UIKit app?" UIHostingController, child containment if partial, closures or observable view model for communication, or UIHostingConfiguration in cells.
  5. "How do you use UIKit inside SwiftUI?" UIViewRepresentable: make once, update idempotently, Coordinator for delegates, binding for upward data.
  6. "Retain cycles?" Delegates are weak; closures use [weak self]; verify with deinit logging, Debug Memory Graph, Leaks instrument.
  7. "Why does Auto Layout complain?" Conflicting or ambiguous constraints; priorities; give identifiers; view debugger.
  8. "Is main-thread enforcement compile-time?" In Swift 6, UIKit types are @MainActor, so misuse is a compile error rather than a runtime warning.

A good end-to-end mental model: UIKit is imperative and stateful: you hold references to views and mutate them. SwiftUI is declarative: you describe a function of state. Most interop bugs come from the two models fighting, e.g. a representable holding UIKit state that SwiftUI does not know about, or a UIKit controller mutating a hosted view model on the wrong thread.

Quick comparison for review:

Concern UIKit SwiftUI
UI description Imperative, mutate view objects Declarative, function of state
Layout Auto Layout constraints Proposed size / chosen size layout
Lists Cell reuse, diffable data source List, LazyVStack, identity-based diffing
Events Delegates, target-action Closures, bindings
Memory Class instances, ARC cycles Value-type views, cycles only in models/closures
Min effort for custom drawing draw(_:), CALayer Canvas, Shape

Real examples. Interview loops at large iOS teams (Uber, Airbnb, Meta) commonly ask for a feed screen built with a collection view and image loading, then a follow-up asking how you would embed a SwiftUI component.

Analogy. Explaining UIKit to a Compose developer is like explaining manual transmission to someone raised on automatics: the same destination, but you manage the clutch (state and lifecycle) yourself.

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting method names without saying what they imply for correctness.
  • Not mentioning threading or retain cycles when discussing delegates and closures.
  • Forgetting to say when you would still choose UIKit (maturity, custom layouts, TextKit, performance-critical lists).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• UIKit is the foundation under SwiftUI and under most existing production apps; learn it as a reader first.
  • UIViewController replaces Activity/Fragment but survives rotation; use viewDidLoad once, viewIsAppearing/viewDidAppear for visible work, and cancel in viewDidDisappear.
  • Views are class objects with a backing CALayer; points not pixels; main thread only (compiler-enforced in Swift 6).
  • Auto Layout is constraint solving with intrinsic size and priorities; remember translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false, safe area, and UIStackView.
  • Lists: table or collection view with cell reuse; modern code uses diffable data sources, cell registrations, compositional layout, and UIHostingConfiguration.
  • Delegates must be weak; ARC does not collect cycles. Bridge callbacks to async with continuations resumed exactly once.
  • UIViewRepresentable and UIViewControllerRepresentable bring UIKit into SwiftUI via make, update, Coordinator; UIHostingController brings SwiftUI into UIKit with proper child containment.
  • Migrate legacy code incrementally: tests, SPM modules, view models, hosted SwiftUI screens, then remove storyboards.
  • Items marked verify: viewIsAppearing back-deployment, diffable data source threading guarantees, sizeThatFits representable signature, sizingOptions availability.
